lessons.title: The Premier League ladder
lessons.objective: You can explain how Premier League places decide Europe and relegation.

payload.prompt: Match each league position to what it usually means.

pairs.definition: The usual number of Champions League places for England.
Promoted up to the Premier League.

explanation.summary: Four ladder rungs matter most to fans: the Champions League places at the top, the drop zone at the bottom, and promotion from below.
explanation.sayThisLine: Top four for Europe, bottom three go down.

payload.template: The Premier League has {{teams}} teams and {{relegated}} are relegated each season.

explanation.correct: Correct. Twenty teams compete, and the bottom three go down to the Championship.
explanation.incorrect: The Premier League has 20 clubs, and three teams are relegated to the Championship each season.

payload.prompt: Who won the 2025-26 Premier League title?

options.text: Arsenal
Manchester City
Liverpool

explanation.correct: Arsenal won the 2025-26 title with 85 points, with Manchester City second on 78 and Manchester United third on 71.
explanation.incorrect: Arsenal took the 2025-26 title with 85 points. It was their first league title since the unbeaten 2003-04 season.
explanation.sayThisLine: Arsenal won it with 85 points, that is a proper title.

statement.speaker: Jamie
statement.text: We need top four for Champions League football.

payload.question: What does Jamie mean?

options.text: His team has to finish in the top four places to play in Europe's biggest club competition
His team has already qualified
The team needs to win four matches to qualify
Finishing fourth automatically wins a trophy

payload.translation: A top-four finish in the Premier League earns entry into the Champions League, the most prestigious European club competition.

followUps.line: Is your team close to top four this season?
followUps.why: Continues the conversation about their team's position.

followUps.line: Have they played in the Champions League before?
followUps.why: Opens a question about their club's history.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If uncertain, ask which European competition their team is in this season.

payload.template: England usually gets {{usual}} Champions League places, but a fifth can be added through UEFA's European Performance Spot, which rewards {{reward}}.

options: strong European results by English clubs
gaps.correct: strong European results by English clubs

explanation.correct: Right. Four is the baseline, and a fifth place can be earned when English clubs do well in Europe.
explanation.incorrect: The baseline is four places. UEFA can add a fifth (the European Performance Spot) based on how a country's clubs perform in Europe.
explanation.sayThisLine: Fifth might get in if English clubs do well in Europe.

lessons.title: FA Cup and the pyramid
lessons.objective: You can explain the FA Cup and the English pyramid.

payload.prompt: What makes the FA Cup special compared to the league?

options.text: It pays more money
Non-league and lower-division teams can face Premier League giants in the early rounds
It's played only in summer

explanation.correct: Exactly. The FA Cup is a knockout competition that starts with hundreds of teams from the lower divisions and non-league, creating the possibility of giant-killing moments.
explanation.incorrect: The magic of the FA Cup is that it draws teams from all levels of the English pyramid, so a fifth-tier team could theoretically face a Premier League side.
explanation.sayThisLine: It's the cup, so anything can happen.

statement.speaker: Sarah
statement.text: The cup magic could happen this weekend.

payload.question: What is she talking about?

options.text: An unlikely upset where a smaller team beats a much bigger one
A magical trick will occur during the match
The weekend is guaranteed to be fun
Her team will definitely win

payload.translation: In cup competitions, especially the FA Cup, smaller teams can produce unexpected upsets that feel like magic because they overcome much bigger opponents.

followUps.line: Has your team had a memorable FA Cup run?
followUps.why: Asks about their personal experience with the cup.

followUps.line: What's the biggest upset you can remember?
followUps.why: Invites them to share a famous cup moment.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You don't need to know every cup story, just that upsets happen and fans love them.

payload.prompt: Can a non-league team from the fifth tier or lower enter the FA Cup?

options.text: No, only Premier League and Championship teams
Yes, teams from all levels of the English pyramid can enter
Only teams from the top three divisions

explanation.correct: Yes. The FA Cup is open to hundreds of teams across all divisions of the English football pyramid, from the Premier League down to non-league.
explanation.incorrect: One of the unique features of the FA Cup is that it draws from the entire English pyramid, making giant-killings possible.
explanation.sayThisLine: The cup is open to everyone, that's why upsets happen.

payload.template: The English pyramid runs from the Premier League down through the {{second}}, then League One and League Two, then the {{fifth}} and beyond.

explanation.correct: Right. Championship second, League One third, League Two fourth and the National League fifth. Non-league starts at that fifth rung.
explanation.incorrect: The order is Premier League, Championship, League One, League Two, then the National League at level five, with non-league football below.
explanation.sayThisLine: It runs all the way down, and the FA Cup lets them all meet.

payload.prompt: Match the English trophy to what it is.

pairs.definition: England's historic knockout cup, open to clubs across the whole pyramid.
A knockout cup for Premier League and EFL clubs, often used to rotate squads.
A season-opening match between the league champions and the FA Cup winners.

explanation.summary: England has several trophies, but the FA Cup is the one that lets tiny clubs meet giants.
explanation.sayThisLine: The FA Cup is where the giant-killings happen.

lessons.title: Spending rules and the 2026/27 laws
lessons.objective: You can explain the spending rules and the new law changes fans are discussing.

payload.prompt: What do Premier League spending rules aim to do?

options.text: Make every club spend exactly the same amount
Keep clubs' spending tied to what they earn, so they do not run into serious debt
Give the biggest clubs extra money to spend

explanation.correct: Right. Spending rules tie what clubs spend to what they earn. Breaking them can bring points deductions, as Everton and Nottingham Forest found in 2023-24.
explanation.incorrect: The rules keep spending linked to income to protect clubs from serious debt. Details change over time, so check the current version before quoting a limit.
explanation.sayThisLine: They can only spend what the rules let them, or points come off.

payload.prompt: From 2026/27, can VAR step in on a wrongly awarded corner?

options.text: No, VAR never looks at corners
Yes, but only for an immediate review of a clear error
Yes, always, for as long as it takes

explanation.correct: Correct. From 1 July 2026, VAR can correct clearly wrongly awarded corners, but only through an immediate review, not a long one.
explanation.incorrect: The 2026/27 Laws let VAR correct wrongly awarded corners, but only when it can be done immediately so the game keeps moving.
explanation.sayThisLine: They can fix a bad corner now, but it has to be quick.

statement.speaker: commentator
statement.text: They're stalling but the ref's got the countdown up now.

payload.question: What does this mean?

options.text: The team is deliberately wasting time and the referee is enforcing the new five-second restart countdown
The referee is timing the entire match
The match is ending soon
A goal will be scored in five seconds

payload.translation: The 2026/27 restart countdown forces teams to restart play (throw-in, goal kick) within five seconds, shown visually by the referee, cutting down on deliberate time-wasting.

followUps.line: Does your team need to improve at restarting quickly?
followUps.why: Asks if it affects their play style.

followUps.line: Do you think the countdown makes the game better?
followUps.why: Opens their opinion on the rule change.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If you're unsure, note that the ref's hand signals count down the five seconds.

payload.prompt: Your club wants a big-money striker. What is the smart call?

situation.narrative: Your club is comfortable in mid-table but its finances are tight.

facts.label: Finances
facts.value: Already close to the spending limit

options.label: Sign the striker regardless of the rules
options.consequence: The club risks breaching the spending rules and a points deduction that could cost more than the striker's goals earn.
considerations: Breaching spending rules can bring points deductions
One signing rarely outweighs the risk of losing points

options.label: Sign the cheaper forward and stay inside the limit
options.consequence: The squad improves without breaking the rules, and the club keeps room for the next window.
considerations: Successful clubs build inside their financial limits
Long-term health matters more than one transfer

options.label: Wait a window and reduce losses first
options.consequence: You avoid any breach but the team goes without a striker for a while.
considerations: Patience can open better opportunities later

payload.expertNote: Fans say "we can't afford it" because clubs near their spending limit have to weigh ambition against the risk of a points deduction.
payload.safetyNote: This scenario explains football business rules; it is not financial advice.

payload.prompt: Complete the purpose of the spending rules.
payload.template: Spending rules aim to keep clubs {{a}} and competition {{b}}.

explanation.correct: Right. The point is to stop clubs collapsing under debt and to stop unlimited owner spending from deciding everything.
explanation.incorrect: The rules protect clubs' finances and support fairer competition by limiting how far spending can outrun income.
explanation.sayThisLine: The rules keep the league fair and the clubs stable.
